title: Anthropic Mathematician Says He and Claude Have Proven the Riemann Hypothesis
excerpt: Levent Alpöge's proof exists as 17 million lines of computer-checked code rather than a paper, and the Clay Institute — which offers $1 million for the problem — still lists it as unsolved while review begins.
body:
• Levent Alpöge, a mathematician on Anthropic's technical staff, announced on Friday that he and the company's AI model Claude have produced a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous unsolved problem in mathematics.
  • The proof is not a paper but 17 million lines of code in Lean, a language computers can check line by line; written out as prose, Alpöge says, it would run to more than 250,000 pages.
  • The claim is not yet accepted: hours after the announcement, the Clay Mathematics Institute still listed the hypothesis as unsolved, and its $1 million Millennium Prize is paid only after the institute's own review.
  • The announcement landed a day after Anthropic's record-breaking Nasdaq debut, which priced the company at about $1.5 trillion.

A mathematician who works for Anthropic says he has done, with an AI at his side, what mathematicians have failed to do since 1859. Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, announced on Friday that he and Claude, Anthropic's AI model, have discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis — the conjecture about the distribution of prime numbers that the Clay Mathematics Institute counts among its seven Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1 million award.

Alpöge made the announcement in a four-page explanation posted on his website, according to CNN. He said the final pieces came together late on Sunday night, and that he messaged Anthropic's chief executive, Dario Amodei, to ask about his "ability to announce" just as the company was preparing its stock market debut. Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq on November 19 after pricing its initial public offering at $83 a share; CNN reported the offering raised a record $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation.

A proof no human can read cover to cover

The proof does not exist as a conventional paper. Alpöge released it as 17 million lines of Lean code — a programming language in which mathematical arguments are written so that a computer can verify each step. Engadget reported that he worked with Claude on the proof over the course of six weeks, and that the complete argument, spelled out in ordinary prose, would run to more than 250,000 pages, because the AI sets out even elementary steps in full.

That format is the story as much as the result. Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and chair of mathematics at Rutgers University, told CNN that a traditional paper is itself "kind of code for a proof" that a reader must follow line by line. Of the machine-checked version, he said Claude had followed the code and pronounced the proof true. "Does that mean I understand it? Not yet. But the computer is extraordinarily picky, way pickier than I am and so if you can satisfy the computer, there's a very, very good chance you're going to satisfy me too," Kontorovich said. "But I have to do the work."

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."

— Levent Alpöge, Anthropic

Alpöge himself was candid that he is "presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics," as CNN quoted him. The Wall Street Journal reported that the organisations behind the Lean ecosystem — the Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative — said on Saturday, after verifying the code, that they have "full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct." Engadget reported that Oxford mathematician James Maynard told The New York Times he was "98 or 99 percent certain" the discovery is accurate.

What has to happen before it counts

None of that settles the matter officially. Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute's website, CNN reported, and the institute's president, Martin Bridson, counselled patience. "This is an announcement of historic significance, which holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics," Bridson said in a statement. "But the journey from today's announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult."

The claim is the second of its kind in recent months. CNN noted that in September, OpenAI said its technology was key to a similar breakthrough on the Navier-Stokes problem, another Millennium Prize Problem, and Engadget reported that OpenAI had also posted progress toward the Riemann Hypothesis in October. For readers, the practical position is simple: a proof has been claimed and machine-checked, mathematicians are broadly optimistic, and the formal verdict — and the $1 million prize — now rests with the Clay Institute's review process, which has no announced timetable.
